STOCK CERTIFICATES AND UNCERTIFICATED SHARES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — STOCK CERTIFICATES AND UNCERTIFICATED SHARES INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme, Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of California. It describes the rules the California Corporations Code sets for how a California corporation may evidence a shareholder's ownership of shares — whether by issuing a physical, signed stock certificate or by using an uncertificated (book-entry) system instead — along with what a certificate or its uncertificated equivalent must state when shares are classified, and how a corporation may replace a certificate that is lost, stolen, or destroyed.

This information sheet is educational only. It states the applicable statutes as written; it does not recommend whether Acme, Inc. should issue certificated or uncertificated shares, does not draft or format any specific certificate or shareholder notice, and does not determine which state's law governs Acme, Inc. if Acme, Inc. was not organized in California or does not otherwise have California as its internal-affairs state. This document is not this project's Corporate Bylaws or Close Corporation documents, which govern a corporation's internal affairs and (for an electing close corporation) its own additional certificate-legend requirement; this document instead focuses specifically on the general certificate-mechanics statutes in Chapter 4 of the General Corporation Law.

EVERY SHAREHOLDER'S DEFAULT ENTITLEMENT TO A CERTIFICATE, AND WHO MAY SIGN IT
Under California law, every holder of shares in a corporation is entitled to have a certificate issued in the corporation's name, certifying the number of shares and the class or series of shares that shareholder owns. The certificate must be signed by two categories of officer acting together: (1) the chairperson or vice chairperson of the board, or the president or a vice president; and (2) the chief financial officer or an assistant treasurer, or the secretary or any assistant secretary. Any or all of these required signatures may be a facsimile signature rather than an original. A certificate signed, or facsimile-signed, by someone who held the required office (or was the transfer agent or registrar) at the time of signing remains valid even if that person has since left that position by the time the certificate is actually issued.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Every holder of shares in a corporation shall be entitled to have a certificate signed in the name of the corporation by the chairperson or vice chairperson of the board or the president or a vice president and by the chief financial officer or an assistant treasurer or the secretary or any assistant secretary, certifying the number of shares and the class or series of shares owned by the shareholder. Any or all of the signatures on the certificate may be facsimile."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 416(a), California General Corporation Law, entitlement to a signed certificate and required officer signatures (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=416.)
  "In case any officer, transfer agent or registrar who has signed or whose facsimile signature has been placed upon a certificate has ceased to be such officer, transfer agent or registrar before such certificate is issued, it may be issued by the corporation with the same effect as if such person were an officer, transfer agent or registrar at the date of issue."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 416(a), California General Corporation Law, a certificate signed by a since-departed officer remains valid (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=416.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 416(a)), used as evidence of the actual statutory floor for a shareholder's default entitlement to a certificate and the officers who must sign it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's certificate-signature rule is the same. Both quotes below are drawn from the same subdivision, § 416(a), and are not independent of one another; they are presented as one source describing two related rules within that subdivision (the signature requirement, and the former-officer validity rule). This default entitlement yields to Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b), under which a corporation may instead adopt an uncertificated system in place of issuing any certificates at all — that alternative is covered in a separate clause of this document rather than here.

CALIFORNIA DOES NOT REQUIRE PHYSICAL CERTIFICATES — UNCERTIFICATED (BOOK-ENTRY) SHARES ARE PERMITTED
California law does not require a corporation to issue physical share certificates for every shareholder. Notwithstanding a shareholder's default entitlement to a signed certificate, a corporation may instead adopt a system for issuing, recording, and transferring its shares by electronic or other means that does not involve issuing any certificates at all — commonly described as uncertificated or book-entry shares. Such a system must include provisions for giving purchasers written notice in substitution for the information that would otherwise appear on a certificate under the statutes governing certificate content and dissenting-share endorsement, and it must also satisfy at least one of three conditions: approval by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, authorization under a federal statute, or compliance with Division 8 of the California Commercial Code. If a corporation has already issued physical certificates for its outstanding shares, a newly adopted uncertificated system does not take effect as to those already-certificated shares until the certificates for them have been surrendered to the corporation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a corporation may adopt a system of issuance, recordation and transfer of its shares by electronic or other means not involving any issuance of certificates, including provisions for notice to purchasers in substitution for the required statements on certificates under Sections 417, 418, and 1302, and as may be required by the commissioner in administering the Corporate Securities Law of 1968, which system (1) has been approved by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, (2) is authorized in any statute of the United States, or (3) is in accordance with Division 8 (commencing with Section 8101) of the Commercial Code."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b), California General Corporation Law, a corporation may adopt an uncertificated (electronic) share system (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=416.)
  "Any system so adopted shall not become effective as to issued and outstanding certificated securities until the certificates therefor have been surrendered to the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b), California General Corporation Law, an uncertificated system is not effective against already-issued certificates until surrender (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=416.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b)), used as evidence that certificated shares are not mandatory in California and that a corporation may instead use an uncertificated system — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction permits uncertificated shares on the same terms. The two quotes below are both drawn from the single subdivision § 416(b) and are not independent of one another; they are one source describing two parts of the same rule (the conditions for adopting an uncertificated system, and the surrender requirement for shares that were already certificated). This document does not independently verify the separate California Commercial Code Division 8 (Investment Securities) requirements that would apply to an uncertificated system relying on that route, and does not verify what the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation currently requires in administering the Corporate Securities Law of 1968 — both are referenced by name in the statute's text but were not independently confirmed against their own primary sources here; an attempted direct fetch of California Commercial Code § 8408 did not return usable statutory text and that specific point is omitted rather than guessed at.

WHAT A CERTIFICATE (OR ITS UNCERTIFICATED EQUIVALENT) MUST STATE WHEN SHARES ARE CLASSIFIED
If a corporation's shares are classified into different classes, or if any class of shares has two or more series, the certificate — or, for uncertificated shares, the initial transaction statement and written statements the corporation sends the shareholder in its place — must contain one of three things: a full statement of the rights, preferences, privileges, and restrictions granted to or imposed on each class or series and its holders; a summary of those rights, preferences, privileges, and restrictions that references the specific provisions of the articles of incorporation and any certificate of determination establishing them; or a statement identifying the corporate office or agency from which a shareholder may obtain a copy of the full statement, on request and without charge.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If the shares of the corporation are classified or if any class of shares has two or more series, there shall appear on the certificate or, in the case of uncertificated securities, the initial transaction statement and written statements, one of the following: (a) A statement of the rights, preferences, privileges and restrictions granted to or imposed upon each class or series of shares authorized to be issued and upon the holders thereof. (b) A summary of such rights, preferences, privileges and restrictions with reference to the provisions of the articles and any certificates of determination establishing the same. (c) A statement setting forth the office or agency of the corporation from which shareholders may obtain, upon request and without charge, a copy of the statement referred to in subdivision (a)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 417, California General Corporation Law, required disclosure of class and series rights on the certificate or its uncertificated equivalent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=417.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 417), used as evidence of the actual required content for a corporation with more than one class or series of shares — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim that a single-class corporation with no series has any obligation under this particular section. This clause does not address the separate, additional statutory content requirements under Cal. Corp. Code § 418(a)-(b) for share-transfer restrictions, redemption rights, voting agreements, irrevocable proxies, or assessability and partly-paid status — this project's Buy-Sell Agreement document separately covers the § 418(a)(1) transfer-restriction-disclosure point for its own purpose, and that ground is not duplicated here. This clause also does not address the separate, stricter close-corporation certificate legend under Cal. Corp. Code § 418(c)-(d), which this project's Close Corporation document covers.

REPLACING A LOST, STOLEN, OR DESTROYED CERTIFICATE
California law lets a corporation issue a new share certificate to replace one that was lost, stolen, or destroyed. Before doing so, the corporation may require the certificate's owner — or the owner's legal representative — to give the corporation a bond or other adequate security, sufficient to indemnify the corporation against any claim, including any expense or liability, arising from the alleged loss, theft, or destruction of the original certificate or from issuing the new one. If a corporation refuses to issue a replacement certificate, the owner or the owner's legal representative may bring an action in superior court for an order requiring the corporation to issue one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A domestic or foreign corporation may issue a new share certificate or a new certificate for any other security in the place of any certificate theretofore issued by it, alleged to have been lost, stolen or destroyed, and the corporation may require the owner of the lost, stolen or destroyed certificate or the owner’s legal representative to give the corporation a bond (or other adequate security) sufficient to indemnify it against any claim that may be made against it (including any expense or liability) on account of the alleged loss, theft or destruction of any such certificate or the issuance of such new certificate."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 419(a), California General Corporation Law, a corporation may issue a replacement certificate and require indemnification security (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=419.)
  "If a corporation refuses to issue a new share certificate or other certificate in place of one theretofore issued by it, or by any corporation of which it is the lawful successor, alleged to have been lost, stolen or destroyed, the owner of the lost, stolen or destroyed certificate or the owner’s legal representative may bring an action in the superior court of the proper county for an order requiring the corporation to issue a new certificate in place of the one lost, stolen or destroyed."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 419(b), California General Corporation Law, a court may order reissuance if the corporation refuses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=419.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 419(a)-(b)), used as evidence of the actual replacement procedure and the corporation's ability to require indemnification security before reissuing a certificate — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. The two quotes below, from § 419(a) and § 419(b), are subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; they are treated as one source describing two branches of the same procedure — the corporation issuing a replacement voluntarily under subdivision (a), or a shareholder seeking a court order under subdivision (b) if the corporation refuses. This document does not describe subdivision (c)'s further detail on what a court must find before ordering reissuance or the bond it may direct the plaintiff to post, and does not address whether or how an equivalent replacement procedure applies to a lost or misappropriated written notice for uncertificated shares — Section 419's text refers only to a "certificate," and that gap is not resolved here.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — STOCK CERTIFICATES AND UNCERTIFICATED SHARES INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme, Inc. was prepared in connection with Jordan Lee's status as the holder of record of 1,000 shares of common stock.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

It does not itself constitute a stock certificate, an initial transaction statement, or a written notice under any of the statutes it describes, does not determine what Acme, Inc.'s own articles, bylaws, or share records currently provide, and does not constitute legal advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]
